9494:
The New Testament contains strong assurances that Christ will keep those the Father gives him, and also sharp warnings that some who have tasted the heavenly gift may fall away. Every tradition must account for both kinds of text, and each does so differently.

The Reformed doctrine of the perseverance of the saints (Synod of Dort, 1619; Westminster Confession chapter 17) holds that all whom God has truly regenerated will persevere in faith to the end, kept by God; those who finally fall away were never truly regenerate. The Arminian and Wesleyan doctrine of conditional security holds that believers are secure while they remain in Christ by faith, but can genuinely abandon faith and be lost. The Free Grace view, a strand of popular once-saved-always-saved teaching shaped by Zane Hodges and Charles Ryrie, holds that anyone who has once believed is eternally saved regardless of later fruit or even continued belief, with the warnings referring to rewards, discipline or discipleship. Catholic and Orthodox churches teach that grace received in baptism can be lost by grave (mortal) sin and restored through repentance and, in Catholic teaching, the sacrament of penance; final perseverance is a gift no one can presume.

The debate concerns not only the warnings but assurance, the nature of saving faith, the relationship between justification and sanctification, and the pastoral care of those who drift.

In Reformed theology, God's saving work is a single chain from election to glorification. Those whom God effectually calls and regenerates he also keeps; they may fall into serious sin for a time, grieve the Spirit and lose the felt assurance of salvation, but they cannot totally or finally fall from grace. Their perseverance depends not on their own free will but on the unchangeable election of the Father, the merit and intercession of Christ, the indwelling Spirit and the nature of the covenant of grace.

The warning passages are real and addressed to real people. Reformed theologians typically read them either as describing people who professed faith and experienced the church's blessings without being regenerate (1 John 2:19), or as the very means God uses to keep his elect persevering (Schreiner and Caneday). Perseverance is therefore not passivity: true believers persevere because God works in them to will and to work.

Augustine's controversy with Pelagians and with monks in Gaul produced the first developed doctrine of the gift of perseverance. The Reformers, especially Calvin, linked it to election and to Christ's intercession, and taught that true faith, though it may be weakened, is never extinguished.

The doctrine was formalized in response to the Remonstrants, whose 1610 articles left open whether believers could fall away. Dort (1619) made perseverance the fifth of its heads of doctrine, the 'P' of the later TULIP acronym. English Puritans and the Westminster Assembly adopted it, and it remains the standard teaching of Reformed, Presbyterian and Reformed Baptist churches. In the twentieth century it was distinguished from the popular once-saved-always-saved teaching by its insistence that true faith perseveres in holiness.

Conditional security holds that believers are fully secure in Christ while they continue in faith, and that no external power can snatch them away, but that a believer can freely turn away from Christ in persistent unbelief and so be lost. Salvation is not earned by perseverance, but it is received and kept through faith, and faith is a living relationship that can be abandoned.

The warnings of Hebrews, Jesus' vine-and-branches teaching and Peter's description of those who escape the world's defilements and then return to it are read at face value as describing genuine believers. Wesleyans add that sin can wound and, if persisted in, destroy the believer's relationship with God, but that God graciously restores the repentant. Some Reformed Arminians (for example many Free Will Baptists) hold that apostasy occurs only through unbelief, not through sin as such, and is irreversible, following Hebrews 6.

The Free Grace position holds that eternal life is given freely to anyone who believes in Jesus for it, at the moment of believing, and that it can never be lost, because it rests on Christ's promise rather than on anything the believer does afterward. Good works, ongoing faithfulness and even continued belief are not conditions or necessary evidences of eternal salvation; they belong to discipleship, which is a separate, costly call for those already saved.

Warning passages are therefore read as threatening loss of rewards, temporal discipline or physical death, or loss of fellowship and fruitfulness, not loss of eternal life. A believer can be 'carnal' and unfruitful yet saved, 'as through fire' (1 Cor 3:15). Advocates such as Zane Hodges argued that this is the only way to keep grace truly free and assurance truly sure. Charles Ryrie defended a more moderate version, holding that every believer will bear some fruit but that fruit is not a test that defines saving faith. The position is distinct from Reformed perseverance, though both affirm eternal security.

Eternal security has long been a popular Baptist conviction ('once saved, always saved'), often held without the full Reformed framework of election. In the twentieth century, dispensational teachers at Dallas Theological Seminary developed a sharp distinction between salvation (a free gift by faith) and discipleship or the Christian life (where rewards, obedience and lordship apply).

The distinction became a public controversy when John MacArthur's *The Gospel According to Jesus* (1988) argued that the gospel calls for repentance and submission to Christ as Lord and that genuine faith inevitably produces obedience. Hodges' *Absolutely Free!* and Ryrie's *So Great Salvation* (both 1989) replied. Michael Horton's edited volume *Christ the Lord* (1992) defended the Reformation's view against Free Grace. The Free Grace movement later divided over how much content saving faith must have.
